title: Responsive Direct Instruction & Teacher Clarity
subtitle: Clear, brief, well-timed explicit teaching — the part of direct instruction that is high-impact, kept and re-timed rather than eliminated.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Hattie, Visible Learning (teacher clarity; direct instruction) · worked-example effect (Sweller) · NCTM, Principles to Actions · pairs with the “When to Tell” guide here.

blocks.text: Explicit teaching done well: the teacher **names the learning target**, **models or explains clearly**, and **checks for understanding** — briefly, and at the moment students are ready to receive it.

“Teacher Clarity” (clear learning intentions and success criteria) and well-structured direct instruction are among the highest-effect-size practices in Hattie’s research synthesis. This tool is the partner to the cross-cutting **“When to Tell”** guide: that guide decides *when* to tell; this one is about telling *well* when you do.

blocks.title: We are not anti-telling — we are anti-mistimed telling

blocks.text: The framework re-times direct instruction; it does not remove it. The most powerful instance is the **consolidation** after a task — that IS direct instruction, landing when students have the hooks to hang it on. There are also brief mid-task tells (a convention, a notation) and short, clear mini-lessons. The goal is brief, clear, and timed — never the eliminated 30–40 minute monologue.

blocks.label: Strands of Mathematical Proficiency
items: Procedural fluency
Conceptual understanding

rows: Students know *what* they’re learning and *why* it matters — stated in student-friendly language.
Students know what “got it” looks like — how they’ll know they’ve learned it.
A concise model with the thinking made visible, not just the steps.
Quick evidence that it landed — before moving on (see the CFU tool).

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: A clear learning target students can restate
A short, well-structured worked example with the reasoning shown
The “tell” landing after struggle, in the consolidation
A quick check before moving on
Explanation broken up with student thinking, not a monologue

no.title: We should *not* see
items: 30+ minutes of teacher talk to open the lesson
Steps with no *why* (“just do this, then this”)
Telling before students have grappled with a derivable idea
“Any questions? No? Moving on” as the only check
A hidden or unstated learning goal

blocks.text: Teacher clarity is one of the highest-impact practices — but “clear” means *students* are clear on the target, the reasoning, and what success looks like. A long, polished lecture can be perfectly delivered and still leave students unclear and passive. Brief + checked beats long + admired.

items: **Explicit learning intentions and success criteria** are an equity move — they remove the hidden curriculum, so students who can’t infer “what the teacher wants” aren’t disadvantaged.
**Worked examples** (with thinking shown) reduce cognitive load and are especially supportive for students with IEPs and for novices building fluency.
**Brief, anchored tells** after struggle keep MLLs and strugglers in the thinking instead of front-loading a wall of language.

sections.label: Lesson design connection
sections.sources: Sources: Hattie, Visible Learning · Sweller (worked examples) · NCTM, Principles to Actions · pairs with “When to Tell” and the 5 Practices here.

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson
Direct instruction is a **mode** woven through Core, not a phase that opens it. It shows up in three places — mostly *after* students think.

rows: After a task, formalize the math from selected student work — name it, notate it, connect it. This is the most powerful direct instruction you do.
A quick convention, notation, or vocabulary a group can’t derive — given on the spot, then hand the thinking back.
When the content is convention-heavy or a procedure needs efficient modeling *after* the concept is understood.

items: **State the target:** “We’re learning to… so that…” (and the success criteria).
**Model the thinking, not just the steps:** narrate *why* at each move (“I need a common denominator *because* the pieces are different sizes”).
**Make one deliberate error or decision visible** so students see reasoning, not a flawless performance.
**Check for understanding** immediately (a quick problem, a thumbs-and-explain).
**Hand it back:** “Now you try the next one” — keep the doing with students.

blocks.title: Use the “When to Tell” guide to decide

blocks.text: Before you explain, run the decision: is this a convention/notation they can’t derive, or consolidation after struggle? **Tell.** Is it an idea they could reason to with a hint? **Hold** — ask a question instead. This guide is what keeps “responsive” honest.

yes.title: Do
items: Post the learning target in student language
Show the reasoning behind the steps
Break the tell with a turn-and-talk or quick check
Anchor it in student work from the task
Stop and hand back the thinking

no.title: Don’t
items: Open with a long lecture before any student thinking
List steps with no why
Talk past the point students stopped following
Treat “no questions” as evidence of understanding
Re-teach your method instead of using theirs (in consolidation)
**Make success criteria explicit and visible** — it levels the field for students who can’t read the “hidden rules” of school.
**Worked examples with visible reasoning** support students with IEPs and reduce working-memory load.
**Keep tells short and anchored** so MLLs aren’t asked to process a long stretch of academic language before doing any mathematics.

blocks.text: Done this way, direct instruction stops being the thing reform “replaces” and becomes a precise, high-impact tool teachers reach for at the right moment. It reassures veterans that their expertise still matters — and it makes the consolidation of every rich task land.
